idea: Rewrite select() as a filter-then-rank pipeline. (1) Drop exact duplicates by hashing normalized text (lowercase, collapse whitespace). (2) Drop junk: documents whose share of non-ASCII characters exceeds 2%, documents containing spam markers such as "discount code", "coupon", "cheap", "buy now", "free shipping", "click here", and documents without a Wikipedia-style "= Title =" header line. (3) Fit a TfidfVectorizer (word unigrams and bigrams, sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2) on target_sample plus the surviving pool, compute each pool document's cosine similarity to the centroid of the target_sample vectors, and sort descending by that score. Return the sorted indices with no repeats. Seed any tie-breaking shuffle from CURATE_SEED. Keep the whole list so the trainer still reads up to T tokens, and let it cycle only if the filtered list is short.
why: The pool is about 2T tokens of which a large share is SEO spam, mojibake, duplicates and off-domain text, while the target is clean Wikipedia-style articles, so removing junk and putting the articles most similar to the target sample first should make the 9.8M training tokens much closer in distribution to the held-out set and lower dev bpb.
outcome: dev 1.9060 against 1.9583 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: After the existing TF-IDF ranking, add a greedy near-duplicate filter. Walk the ranked survivors in order, keep a doc only if its cosine similarity to every already-kept doc is below 0.8 (use the same L2-normalized TF-IDF matrix, computing each candidate's dot products against the kept matrix in chunks to stay within 180 s). Append the dropped near-duplicates at the end of the returned list, in their ranked order, so the output still contains every surviving index and the trainer can still read T tokens. Keep the seeded tie-breaking shuffle as is.
why: The pool is about 2T tokens of noisy text with templated and near-identical variants that exact-hash dedup misses (for example, lightly edited copies of the same article or spam template), so the top-ranked half that the trainer actually reads is likely full of redundant text, and removing near-duplicates should add diversity within the T-token budget and improve held-out bpb.
outcome: dev 1.9044 against 1.9060 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Add a word-order garbling filter after the junk filter and before TF-IDF ranking. For each surviving doc, lowercase and tokenize into words, form its word bigrams, and compute coverage = fraction of those bigrams that also occur in the bigram set built from target_sample (ignoring bigrams containing non-alphabetic tokens). Compute coverage for all survivors, then drop the bottom 10% by coverage (percentile cutoff, so no absolute threshold needs tuning). Keep the rest in the existing TF-IDF ranking and seeded tie-break. Do not drop any doc whose token count is below 50, since short docs have noisy coverage.
why: Pool docs such as the scrambled "( a English released George album the It..." article are damaged word-order text that passes the header, non-ASCII and spam checks, and the TF-IDF unigram/bigram ranking does not penalize them, so a bigram-coverage check against the clean target text should remove this damage the current filters miss.
outcome: dev 1.9181 against 1.9060 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), replace the single-centroid score with a kNN-style score. Keep steps (1) dedup and (2) junk filter unchanged, and keep the TF-IDF fit on target_sample plus survivors. Compute the L2-normalized target matrix T (200 x V) and survivor matrix D. Set S = D @ T.T (survivors x 200), then score each survivor as the mean of its top-k similarities with k=5 (np.partition on each row, take the 5 largest, average). Sort descending by that score, using the same seeded random.Random(seed) shuffle as a tie-breaker before the stable sort. Return the ordered survivor indices with no repeats.
why: The centroid averages away the target's topical spread (battles, novels, albums, and so on), so a document that closely matches one specific target article can rank low, whereas scoring each pool document by its top-k matches to individual target articles should pull in a broader, more on-distribution set for the roughly first half of the pool that the trainer actually consumes within T tokens.
outcome: dev 1.9293 against 1.9060 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Add a surface-format filter after the junk filter and before TF-IDF ranking. For each surviving doc, compute fmt = (number of whitespace-separated tokens that are pure punctuation or the token "@-@", e.g. ",", ".", "(", ")", ":", ";", "@-@") divided by total whitespace-separated tokens. Compute the same statistic for every target_sample doc and set cutoff = 10th percentile of those target values. Drop any survivor with fmt < cutoff, and do not drop docs with fewer than 50 tokens. Keep the remaining survivors in the existing TF-IDF centroid ranking and seeded tie-break, and keep the rest of select() unchanged.
why: The target articles are WikiText-style text with detokenized spacing (" , ", " . ", " @-@ ", " ( "), and bpb is measured per byte, so pool docs whose punctuation layout does not match this style, such as the Q&A and web text, would teach the model a byte distribution the held-out set does not use, and a percentile cutoff from the target sample avoids hand-tuning a threshold.
outcome: dev 1.9162 against 1.9060 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the same filter and TF-IDF ranking, but change the output order to ascending score (most target-like last). Concretely: walk the descending-ranked list, accumulate whitespace-token counts until they reach about T tokens, take that prefix as the selected set, then reverse that prefix so the highest-scoring documents appear at the end of the stream. Keep the seeded tie-break. No new filters.
why: The trainer reads in order and stops after T tokens, so the current ranking spends the budget on the best documents early and leaves the most target-like text at the start of training; placing the closest-to-target documents last should favor the final low-learning-rate steps and recency, and this ordering change has not been tried.
outcome: dev 1.9783 against 1.9060 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), change the TfidfVectorizer so it keeps punctuation and the WikiText-style "@-@" / "@,@" / "@.@" joiner tokens instead of discarding them. Replace the default token_pattern with token_pattern=r"[^\s]+" (leave lowercase=True, ngram_range=(1,2), sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2 unchanged), so the fit on target_sample plus survivors and the centroid cosine ranking see tokens such as "@-@", "(", ")", ",", "." and "=". Keep dedup, junk filter, seeded tie-break and the rest of select() as they are.
why: The target documents use WikiText-103 tokenization (for example "20 @.@ 37 miles", "( MD 18 )", "= Title ="), and the default token pattern throws away the punctuation and "@-@" joiners that mark that format, so the current ranking cannot tell pool documents in the same tokenized style apart from differently formatted ones; keeping those tokens should make the centroid score pick the target's format as well as its topic, without adding a hard filter like the rejected surface-format experiment.
outcome: dev 1.8875 against 1.9060 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Add a character-garbling filter after the junk filter and before TF-IDF ranking. For each surviving doc, lowercase it and split on whitespace, stripping leading and trailing non-alphabetic characters from each token. Count how many pool-wide document frequencies each token has by building a Counter of the set of stripped tokens across all deduplicated pool docs (df). A token is "common" if df >= 3. Compute garble = fraction of the doc's alphabetic tokens that are common. Exempt docs with fewer than 50 tokens. Among the rest, drop the bottom 10% by garble (percentile cutoff, no absolute threshold). Keep everything else unchanged: the TF-IDF centroid ranking, the seeded tie-break, and the output list of indices with no repeats.
why: The pool contains scrambled-letter and damaged documents (for example "We tgo a iprtme to uct nowd" and "tihW tsreof viseerc"), and their made-up tokens are rare across the pool, so a unigram rarity signal should catch them directly, where the earlier bigram-coverage filter (experiment 3) only measured target-vocabulary overlap and was rejected.
outcome: dev 1.8954 against 1.8875 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), after the junk filter and before the TF-IDF fit, drop every surviving doc with fewer than 200 whitespace-separated tokens (a hard minimum length, not a percentile). Keep the rest of the pipeline unchanged: TF-IDF fit on target_sample plus survivors with token_pattern=r"[^\s]+", centroid cosine ranking, seeded tie-break, and the full output list of indices with no repeats. If the length filter leaves no survivors, fall back to the current behaviour (no length filter).
why: Short fragments (product-listing spam, one-line stubs, scraped snippets) can score high on centroid cosine because they are dominated by a few target-like terms, so a minimum article length should remove them without touching the header or junk logic, and the 2T pool leaves plenty of full-length articles to fill the T-token budget.
outcome: dev 1.8881 against 1.8875 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Keep the existing filters and TF-IDF centroid ranking unchanged, then upsample the most target-like documents. After computing the descending-score order, take the top 10% of ranked survivors (by score) and prepend a second copy of them, so the stream is [top10%] + [full ranked list]. Accumulate whitespace-token counts and truncate the stream once it reaches about T tokens, so the lowest-ranked docs are the ones dropped. Keep the seeded tie-break and allow the repeated indices, since select() may return repeats.
why: Experiments 1 and 7 show that ranking by similarity to the target helps, and the trainer reads only the first T tokens of the list, so the least target-like documents are never reached. Repeating the closest 10% of documents should shift more of the 300-step budget toward the target distribution, and that is a different lever from the ordering tweaks already tried (reversal, kNN scoring, near-duplicate removal).
outcome: dev 1.8887 against 1.8875 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), keep everything else as in the current best (dedup, junk filter, token_pattern=r"[^\s]+", seeded tie-break), but change the TfidfVectorizer call to add stop_words="english" and max_df=0.3 (keep ngram_range=(1,2), sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2). Stop words and terms that occur in more than 30% of documents are removed from the feature space, so the centroid cosine ranking depends on topical content words rather than function words and generic Wikipedia phrasing.
why: The current ranking is likely dominated by high-frequency function words and generic formatting tokens that make any Wikipedia-style article look similar to the target centroid, so pruning them should sharpen the ranking toward target-specific content.
outcome: dev 1.9584 against 1.8875 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: In select(), keep dedup, junk filter, the TfidfVectorizer call (token_pattern=r"[^\s]+", ngram_range=(1,2), sublinear_tf=True, min_df=2), and the seeded tie-break unchanged. Replace the ranking score with a background-contrastive score: compute target_centroid as the normalized mean of the L2-normalized target_sample vectors, and pool_centroid as the normalized mean of the L2-normalized survivor vectors. For each survivor set score = cos(doc, target_centroid) - 0.5 * cos(doc, pool_centroid). Sort descending by score with the same seeded random.Random(seed) shuffle applied before a stable sort, and return the full ordered survivor list with no repeats.
why: The current centroid score ranks documents that are generically "Wikipedia-like" as highly as those specifically about target-style topics, and subtracting the pool-average direction should push up documents whose similarity to the target is distinctive rather than shared by all pool text, while keeping the one change that has helped so far (punctuation-preserving tokens) and avoiding the rejected kNN, stop-word, and max_df variants.
outcome: dev 1.8879 against 1.8875 for the best at the time, rejected
